content: A nabothian cyst is a mucus-filled cyst that forms on the surface of the cervix. These cysts typically develop when new tissue growth obstructs the nabothian glands, leading to the entrapment of mucosal secretions in small subdermal pockets. The size of these cysts usually ranges from 2 to 10 millimeters in diameter. Nabothian cysts are also referred to as nabothian follicles, mucinous retention cysts, or epithelial inclusion cysts. They are named after Martin Naboth, a German anatomist who described them in his 1707 treatise titled De sterilitate mulierum. However, these cysts were first documented earlier by Guillaume Desnoues, a French surgeon. Clinically, nabothian cysts often present as firm, raised bumps on the surface of the cervix. Women may notice these cysts during self-examinations, such as when inserting a diaphragm or cervical cap, or as part of fertility awareness practices. Gynecologists frequently identify these cysts during routine pelvic examinations. Nabothian cysts are generally harmless and tend to resolve spontaneously. Some women observe that the cysts appear and disappear in correlation with their menstrual cycle. If a woman detects an unusual anomaly on her cervix and is uncertain whether it is a nabothian cyst, consulting a physician is advised to exclude other potential conditions. In some cases, multiple large nabothian cysts may be identified, and imaging techniques such as CT or MRI can be utilized for further evaluation. Treatment for nabothian cysts is typically unnecessary unless the cysts grow significantly large and cause secondary symptoms. In such cases, a gynecologist may perform a colposcopy or biopsy to rule out malignancy or other underlying issues. If removal is deemed necessary, two common methods include electrocautery and cryotherapy. Complications associated with nabothian cysts are rare. However, in some instances, they may be linked to chronic cervicitis, which is an inflammatory condition of the cervix.
